A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Moving Out and BASS, with matching authors, tasks and method. All 24 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v3, including appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures supporting reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original AI-AI experiments, human-AI evaluations, questionnaire outcomes, component ablations and simulator comparisons in Section 6 and the appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental and human-study results and adds participant-disjoint evaluations, dataset-diversity measurements and BASS module analyses.

M1.justification: BASS retains partner-pose perturbation, sub-trajectory recombination, learned latent dynamics, partner-action prediction and NFD-based action selection. The detailed augmentation formulation moves to Appendix O. Newly specified sampling details and diagnostic alternatives do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same two Moving Out tasks, 12 maps, student and expert cohorts, and Overcooked Cramped Room test. The added diversity diagnostics examine human, expert and MAPPO behavior within existing coverage; participant-disjoint splits change the evaluation protocol.

E2.justification: The main MLP, GRU, DP and MAPPO comparators remain. V3 additionally evaluates GRU and the previously cited qVAE as alternative next-state predictors, and introduces random-state and random-partner-action controls in Appendix L. These expand module-level comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 supplements v1's automatic self-play evaluation with separate models trained on disjoint participant groups and compared under same-group and cross-group pairing (Section 4.2; Appendix M). New diagnostic protocols include trajectory-diversity metrics, state-prediction L2 error and partner-action error tolerances. The original four task metrics, including size-weighted TCR, and baseline training settings remain.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial tests of dataset diversity, augmentation validity, sampling strategies, prediction accuracy, random partner actions, alternative dynamics models and NFD versus NFD+AC scoring (Appendices B, H and K-N). A comparative rollout is also added. V1's component ablations, oracle comparison, autoencoder-training analysis and failure cases remain rather than being replaced.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly specifies 20 runs per map with different random seeds; v3 states that AI-AI results average 20 runs without retaining those qualifiers. Standard-error reporting and the independent t-test with p = 0.017 persist. This is a limited reporting change, not evidence of an increased or reduced run budget.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial result sets while retaining v1 Tables 6-7 as Tables 15-16. Its new Task 1 comparison reports same-group/cross-group TCR of 0.3503/0.3010 for BASS and 0.3233/0.2563 for DP. Further findings include over 99% augmentation validity and new sampling and prediction results. These are added outcomes under additional protocols, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The Dec-MDP formulation, constrained-transition expression, augmentation mathematics and four task-metric formulas are retained. Moving the detailed augmentation formulation to Appendix O and adding informal coherence explanations do not introduce new formal assumptions, proofs or theoretical results.

C1.justification: The benchmark, two-task dataset and BASS performance contributions remain, and the abstract is substantively unchanged. V3 adds an explicit introduction claim that this is the first benchmark with a human-collected dataset designed for continuous, low-level motion control, sharpening the claimed novelty.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands scientific interpretation: endpoint matching is argued to preserve collaborative intent, independent sampling to capture useful joint transitions, and qVAE representations to struggle with fine physical dynamics. Appendices K and N explain performance-latency and task-progress versus force-alignment tradeoffs; Appendix U adds a rationale for map difficulty. The earlier BC/RL interpretations and failure discussion remain.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies the default four-sample policy/partner scheme, numerical Task 2 attribute perturbations of up to 10%, and structured JSON map definitions. Most architecture, optimizer, training-budget, hardware, augmentation-noise and grid-distance details were already documented in v1. The project-page access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds targeted citations on SmartHelp, physical reasoning and single-agent trajectory stitching, explicitly distinguishing BASS's collaborative augmentation. Appendix A expands its comparison to Watch and Help and SmartHelp. Several general robotics, world-model and LLM references are removed, while the central positioning around continuous physical collaboration remains.

P1.justification: V3 substantially rewrites and condenses the introduction and related work, refocuses the experimental narrative around four research questions, and moves detailed augmentation mathematics and the main component-ablation discussion into appendices. It also reorganizes appendix sections and shortens the conclusion's limitations discussion. These are substantial structural edits beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V3 redraws Figure 1, replaces the Task 1 portion of the combined performance figure with a grouped results table, and relocates the original ablation table. It adds randomization examples, trajectory-coverage visualizations, a comparative rollout, an action-consistency diagram and multiple diagnostic tables. The environment-comparison table is also expanded.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses an important gap in v1's automatic evaluation: self-play did not separate seen from unseen partner behavior. Participant-disjoint comparisons, together with direct diversity, augmentation-validity and dynamics checks, substantially strengthen evidence for the benchmark and BASS's central claims. Some new validation details remain sparse, and the pre-existing discrepancy between 32 human-study participants in Section 6.1 and 12 in the appendix persists, limiting reproducibility without outweighing the substantial validation gains.
